newsitem.title: papua new guinea: Papua PM offers olive branch to army rebels.
newsitem.headline: Papua PM offers olive branch to army rebels.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Wednesday offered an olive branch to rebel army officers, saying his government would consider dropping a plan to use mercenaries on Bougainville island.

However, a helicopter pilot from the mercenaries said in Singapore that Papua New Guinea had already cancelled its contract with British-based Sandline International for the hire of the group to help its battle with rebels on the island.

"The contract's terminated. It's as simple as that. It's better for both sides," the pilot, accompanied by five colleagues and who declined to be identified, told reporters while in transit to South Africa.
His comments could not immediately be confirmed. Sandline had used South Africa-based Executive Outcomes to supply the mercenaries.

Chan's statement came after a fresh challenge to his authority on Wednesday as army officers rallied against the use of the mercenaries to quell a nine-year island uprising on Bougainville and a street protest erupted in violence.
Chan said six of the 40 mercenaries left Papua New Guinea on Wednesday. The other 34 remained confined to barracks in the north of the country.

He said he was in complete control of the South Pacific nation, which was thrown into chaos when he sacked the country's army chief who had demanded Chan's resignation over plans to use the mercenaries against seccessionist rebels on Bougainville, 900 km (560 miles) northeast of the capital.
Protesters on Wednesday delivered a petition which called for the mercenaries to be sent home and for Chan to resign.
"The cancellation of Sandline, as demanded by the petition, will be considered by the cabinet," Chan told a news conference. "But we must not be too premature about making that decision.
The helicopter pilot and another pilot said they arrived in Papua New Guinea on Sunday and were told on Monday to leave.

"The contract was stopped by mutual agreement," said one, who added the other 34 mercenaries sent to the country would leave once logistical problems, which he did not specify, were sorted out. Their four colleagues declined to talk to reporters.

In Port Moresby, former army chief Jerry Singirok said on Tuesday he accepted his dismissal but he remained holed up in the capital's main barracks, where at least 1,500 protesters arrived to support him in his campaign against Chan.
Major Walter Enuma said before the protests the defence force still considered Singirok to be its commander and demanded that all the mercenaries leave.

"The mercenaries have come in here and undermined the constitutional rule of this country," Enuma, a handgun in one hand and megaphone in the other, told cheering protesters outside the city's Murray barracks.
Chan said he would not resign and that acting commander Colonel Alfred Aikung was in charge of the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) despite the apparent split in the army.
Protesters had earlier tried to entice soldiers to join them in a march on parliament house but the soldiers cheered them while remaining in barracks.
Violence followed within hours when demonstrators broke loose from the crowd and started looting nearby shops.
In a first wave, about 200 demonstrators attacked two supermarkets. Police fired tear gas into the crowd and live ammunition over their heads to calm the situation.
The demonstration officially ended after the petition was handed to a government minister.
But the bulk of the protesters ran up a main city street to loot another supermarket. Heavily-armed police fired teargas and more live rounds at the looters, forcing them to disperse.
Chan has been criticised internationally over the mercenary plan for resource-rich Bougainville island.
Australia, one of the leading critics, on Wednesday sent a diplomatic mission to Port Moresby to help end the crisis.
In Singapore, the two pilots said they had no regrets in having gone to Papua New Guinea. When asked whether their presence had helped, one said: "Yes, I think it has."
"It was a wake-up call. There were nine years of Bougainville and it should have been stopped a long time ago -- whatever, political, military wise, anything," he said.
